title: Hooks That Get Views: 40 Openers Built to Survive the Swipe
markdown:
# Hooks That Get Views: 40 Openers Built to Survive the Swipe

At 0:02, the viewer’s thumb is already moving. Your video may have a useful point, clean editing, and a strong ending—but none of it matters if the first spoken line gives them no reason to pause.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you ready-to-use hooks that get views by making a specific promise, naming a tension, or opening a gap the viewer wants closed. Pick one that matches the video you actually made, then test it against a second angle.

## Fitness and wellness hooks

- “Stop trying to be motivated. Make this one change instead.”
- “The reason your workout plan keeps failing is probably week one.”
- “You do not need a longer workout—you need this 10-minute rule.”
- “If you restart every Monday, watch this before your next workout.”
- “Most beginner gym plans make this mistake on day one.”
- “I would never tell a beginner to start with this exercise.”
- “Before you buy another supplement, check this.”
- “The habit that made [ADD: your result] easier was not exercise.”

## Money and career hooks

- “This is the sentence I would use to ask for a higher rate.”
- “If your paycheck disappears by the end of the month, start here.”
- “You do not need five side hustles. You need one offer people understand.”
- “Before your next interview, remove this answer from your script.”
- “The budget category I ignored until it cost me [ADD: your number].”
- “A client is not saying no to your price—they may not understand the outcome.”
- “Here is a faster way to decide whether a job offer is actually better.”
- “If your portfolio starts with ‘I am passionate,’ change it today.”

## Food and home hooks

- “I stopped buying this grocery item and cut one decision from every dinner.”
- “This is what I cook when I have [ADD: your time] and no plan.”
- “Your meal prep is taking too long because you are prepping the wrong thing.”
- “Do not organize your kitchen until you try this five-minute test.”
- “The cheapest-looking dinner in my fridge is the one I make first.”
- “If your leftovers keep going bad, this is the step you are skipping.”
- “One drawer caused most of my kitchen clutter.”
- “This recipe starts with the ingredient people usually throw away.”

## Beauty, style, and product hooks

- “This looked expensive until I used it in daylight.”
- “Do not buy this color until you see what it does next to [ADD: skin tone or feature].”
- “The styling trick is not the product—it is where you place it.”
- “I tested the cheaper version so you do not have to guess.”
- “This outfit formula works when you have five minutes to leave.”
- “The before-and-after changes because of one small placement choice.”
- “If your makeup disappears on camera, start with this layer.”
- “This is the detail that makes the whole outfit look unfinished.”

## Creator and business hooks

- “Your video is not boring. Its first sentence is doing no work.”
- “Do not open your tutorial with ‘So today…’”
- “Here is the hook format I use when the topic sounds too ordinary.”
- “You have one sentence to make this video worth watching. Try this.”
- “The mistake is not your editing—it is the promise in your opening line.”
- “Turn a vague tip into a hook with this one question.”
- “If your first three seconds explain the topic, rewrite them.”
- “This is how to make a small result sound specific without making it bigger.”

## How to choose a hook

A hook should fit the proof and payoff already inside your video. Do not choose a contrarian opener if the video cannot explain the reversal. Do not use a number unless you can show where it came from.

Use a question when the viewer likely recognizes the problem: “Why does everyone quit by January 20th?” Use a mistake hook when you can name and correct a common error. Use a contrarian hook when the video challenges an expectation. Use a concrete result hook only when your real number is ready to show.

The strongest choice is usually the narrowest honest promise. “How to save money” is broad. “The grocery decision that stopped my weekday takeout” tells the viewer what they will get and who it is for.

## How to test hooks without changing the whole video

Make two openings for the same video. Keep the topic, proof, and ending the same; change only the first spoken line and its on-screen text. That isolates the opening rather than turning the test into a comparison of two different videos.

Check each version for three things:

1. Can a viewer repeat the promise after one listen?
2. Does the next beat deliver on that promise immediately?
3. Is the on-screen text shorter than the spoken line, rather than a duplicate paragraph?

A hook can create curiosity in different ways: a direct problem, a surprising instruction, a question, a visible before-and-after, or a specific mistake. Build several angles, then choose the one that most accurately introduces the video you have.

## FAQ

### What makes a hook get views?

A useful hook gives the viewer a reason to continue: a problem they recognize, a result they want, a mistake they want to avoid, or a question they want answered. The rest of the video still has to fulfill that promise.

### Should I use a question or a bold statement?

Use a question when recognition is the draw. Use a bold statement when you can support it in the next beat. Neither format fixes a vague topic.

### How long should a short-form hook be?

Aim to make the premise understandable in the opening seconds. If the viewer needs a second explanation before they know why to stay, shorten the line.

### Can I use the same hook format more than once?

Yes. Reuse the structure, not the exact claim. A repeatable format becomes useful when each video supplies a new, truthful tension or proof point.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the input and output format:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.

When you have a topic but not an opening worth filming, give Hook Lab the audience, tone, and video length. It returns positioning, multiple spoken-hook options with matching on-screen text and types, a recommended pick, a script shape, and a caption.
